author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Diagnose a missing left or right PS2 audio channel
summary: Use a stereo control clip, a second PS2 title, route swaps, and earpiece reversal to locate one missing channel without masking it with mono output.
heroAlt: Xenosaga scene selected as a repeatable stereo test point for comparing left and right PS2 audio events

blocks.text: Follow the missing side from source to ear

Select a repeatable in-game scene with a sound that moves clearly from left to right, then play a known stereo identification file through the same Android output. Record the emulator balance, Android accessibility balance and mono setting, connected adapter, and physical speaker or earpiece. This establishes whether the missing side begins inside the title or after the emulator mix.

Do not raise volume or enable mono as a repair. Mono can make both speakers produce sound while concealing that one channel, connector contact, or DAC path is absent. Avoid changing synchronization or latency during this test; those settings affect timing and cannot restore a channel that is being discarded downstream.

items: Known stereo media confirms the route can reproduce both sides.
Android balance, mono audio, and enhancement states recorded.
Second headset or phone speakers available for comparison.
Record Android balance, mono processing, output route, adapter orientation, and a stereo identification file before testing the game mix.
Replay one cue that pans left-center-right, then swap physical earpieces to learn whether the silent side follows hardware or logic.

blocks.text: Change one stereo layer per pass

items: 1. Play the known stereo clip and label the physical left and right outputs.
2. Run the repeatable PS2 scene and record which event is absent.
3. Test a second PS2 title without changing global audio options.
4. Inspect Android balance and mono accessibility settings without enabling them as a workaround.
5. Disconnect the headset or adapter and compare phone speakers.
6. Reverse the earpieces physically to see whether the fault follows hardware.
7. Reconnect the intended route and restart the emulator audio session.
8. Keep a per-game note only if every other source and title passes.

blocks.text: Swap the left and right earpieces or cable ends without changing software. If the silence follows the physical side, inspect the transducer, cable, adapter, or jack. If it stays with the logical channel, compare another PS2 game and the stereo test file, then bypass Bluetooth or HDMI to isolate Android routing from the emulator and title mix.

Confirm three distinct positions—left, center, and right—through the intended output, then disconnect and reconnect that route. Repeat after a cold game boot rather than a save-state restore. The channel assignment must remain correct at moderate volume with Android balance centered and mono processing disabled.

items: Known media and two PS2 scenes produce both channels.
Left and right events arrive on the intended physical sides.
Route reconnect does not drop one side.
Retain both the external stereo-file result and the in-game pan result; together they locate the channel loss before or after emulation.
Reconnect the intended output and cold-boot the game with balance centered; all three positions must return on the correct physical sides.

blocks.text: Stereo patterns and their likely layer

items: The same earpiece is silent for all apps: inspect hardware or connector.
Both sides play identical audio: disable forced mono and recheck.
Only one game lacks a channel: verify its scene and title-specific behavior.
The missing side changes when the plug moves: replace the cable or adapter.

blocks.text: Restore the original output route only after returning balance and accessibility audio options to their recorded values. Remove temporary adapters one at a time and replay the same position cue. Keep the route that reproduces the fault labeled; do not compensate by changing every game's audio or by overwriting a good global configuration.
Game scenes are not always mixed symmetrically

Music and ambience are often mixed near the center and are poor channel tests. Use directional effects or a purpose-built stereo file, and remember that some televisions downmix or process HDMI independently from headphones. The correct conclusion may be a faulty route rather than an emulator setting, so retain both external-media and in-game evidence.
